items.body: The Glorious Assembly Jazz Orchestra is the creation of Emmy Award-winning film composer David Mitcham . After a career writing music for the screen, often with jazz undertones, Mitcham has chosen to expand his ambitions by directing a full-on extended big band playing new compositions on Glorious Assembly. The 20- piece group features some of the UK's top players, with additional specialists on flute, E-flat clarinet, bass and contrabass clarinet, and tuba. The palette is further expanded by performers doubling on various ukuleles, piccolo, alto flutes and echo harmonicas (with two reeds for each set of notes giving an echo effect). The album, recorded in one day at Mark Knopfler's British Grove Studios, sets out Mitcham's stall with eight varied tracks showing a range of sound and style. His background in composing comes to the fore immediately; the tunes develop musically with momentum and grace, as if sliding down a spiraling banister with new ideas waiting on every floor. The soloists are given just enough space within each number, time to state their case with purpose and then depart as a new focus appears. Mitcham clearly has an ear for an evocative melody, as demonstrated by the opening "The Autumn of Our Days." Andy Wood 's gorgeous thematic statement on trombone leads first to a lyrical tenor solo by Mark Lockheart. The feel builds into a well-honed electric guitar solo by John Parricelli and further into Tom Rees-Roberts's full-on trumpet take. The track subsides—but whoever's autumnal days we are talking about, there is clearly life remaining. "335," named for the iconic Gibson model, opens with a riff from Parricelli (playing the selfsame guitar) alongside Loz Garrett's double bass. Gareth Williams takes a turn on piano before sax-swapping and fiery brass take over. Gareth Lockrane 's flute provides the icing on a particularly tasty cake. "Tom Wallager" recalls a John Steinbeck passage from his 1954 novel Sweet Thursday, where the characters decide to have "a Tom Wallager of a party"; wild carousing ensues. It is never made clear who Tom Wallager is, but he is effectively brought to life by this rapid-fire sax/brass interplay led by high E-flat clarinet lines. Phil Meadows seizes the moment on alto sax before Lockrane's flute appears to call a temporary relaxation. The pace picks up again with Claire McInerney having the last hurrah on baritone sax. Every track has treasures to offer. "Gold in the Depths" opens with a wistful piano/arco bass theme with a Latin lilt before a welcome extended flute solo from Lockrane and a fluid trumpet solo from Laura Jurd. "Bop Canon" (strictly more canon than bop, it should be said) is a six-part canon driven by the energetic drums of Ian Thomas, aka 'Ianto.' There is a great deal of smart writing here, reminding me somewhat of Mike Westbrook's large-scale works in its exuberance and rich instrumentation. The group performed in concert at the album launch, and I hope more outings will be possible. The appearance of a new voice in large-group jazz is a welcome addition to 2026.

items.body: When it comes to ragtime jazz, pianist, historian, author, and cultural preservationist Terry Waldo literally wrote the book. Said book is This Is Ragtime (Jazz at Lincoln Center, Inc., 1976), widely regarded as the most thorough and authoritative guide to one of modern jazz's early precursors. Treasury, Volume 3 is the last in a trilogy of recordings by Waldo's Gotham City Band devoted to the best of traditional ragtime music. This is exuberant toe-tapping jazz, radiating happiness and high spirits in every measure, from the impish opening number, "Minnie the Mermaid," to the final measures of Jelly Roll Morton's enticing "Black Bottom Stomp." Even the normally staid "Alice Blue Gown" is gussied up in a radiant new outfit that allows her to sashay rather than stroll. Waldo arranged every number, five of which encompass vocals by Waldo, trombonist Jim Fryer, trumpeter Mike Davis, drummer Jay Lepley, or banjo player Jerron Paxton. The band itself is an octet on five tracks, a septet on the other half-dozen. Besides piano, trombone and rhythm, it includes one (and sometimes two) trumpets—which are actually cornets—as well as clarinet and banjo. Whatever its makeup, the band works extremely well as a unit, and soloists needn't be concerned about any lag in their support. And yes, the various members of the band do improvise, and acquit themselves quite well, keeping in mind that their ad-libs are entrenched in the sort of "Dixieland" parlance that predated bop and even the Swing Era. Morton is represented again by "Kansas City Stomp" and "Frog-i-More Rag"; King Oliver by "Canal Street Blues" and "Mabel's Dream"; and W.C. Handy by "Memphis Blues." Blind Lemon Jefferson's "Take Me Back," Haven Gillespie's "Louisiana Fairy Tale" and Arnett Nelson's "Buddy's Habits" round out the charming program. Waldo's eloquent piano is a constant, as are Fryer's trombone, Brian Nalepka 's steady bass and Lepley's assertive drums. Mike Davis and Colin Hancock share trumpet (cornet) duties, Ricky Alexander and Evan Arntzen are the clarinetists. Paxton (who doubles as vocalist on "Take Me Back"), Nick Russo and Arnt Arntzen the banjoists. Fryer sings on "Minnie the Mermaid" and "Memphis Blues," trumpeter Davis on "Alice Blue Gown," Lepley on "Louisiana Fairy Tale," and each one is a stride or two above the norm. "Tradition is the framework that upholds this wonderful music," Hancock writes in the album's liner notes. "Terry Waldo embodies that tradition, and his music brings it to life." Waldo's Treasury, Volume 3 is a splendid storehouse of music that should never be disparaged or forgotten, and a fun-filled tribute the talented musicians who brought it to life while paving the way for more up-to-date and forward-leaning music yet to come.

items.body: Carlos Henriquez has long understood that rhythm tells stories long before words arrive. On Monk Con Clave, he takes Thelonious Monk's angular brilliance and brings it back to the streets, dance halls, and other crowded spaces across New York's Afro-Caribbean neighbourhoods. The result is not merely a tribute album but a living dialogue between Monk's genius and Henriquez's Nuyorican identity. Leading his self-named big band, Henriquez has assembled a remarkable multigenerational ensemble featuring musicians from the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra, along with the propulsive conguero Pedrito Martinez, the sparkling trumpet of Michael Rodriguez, pianists Gonzalo Rubalcaba, Osmany Paredes, and Robert Rodriguez, vocalist Anthony Almonte, and flautist Jeremy Bosch. Yet despite the star power, the performance succeeds because Henriquez never loses sight of the groove beneath the architecture. "'Round Midnight" opens not at midnight but in atmosphere. The familiar melody floats over layered percussion and brass voicings, with Rubalcaba feeding off the rhythmic texture. Trumpeter Michael Rodriguez offers a brief solo in a warm, centred tone. Henriquez's arrangement avoids sentimentality, letting the rhythm coalesce beneath the harmony. "I Mean You" bolts awake with swagger. Henriquez opens with a big-toned bass foundation, and the brass section punches hard in the follow-up, turning Monk's quirky accents into dance impulses. Paredes jumps into the arrangement, which swings fiercely without sanding off Monk's jagged edges. Henriquez's own compositions, "El Son de Teo" and "San Juan Hill," follow and are among the album's emotional centres. The former is rooted in Afro-Cuban traditions, with the rhythm section honouring that musical ancestry. Bosch brings a folkloric vocal spirit to the performance, and his singing becomes part of the rhythmic fabric, warm and immediate. Rubalcaba is masterful throughout, threading sharp harmonic ideas and flowing montuno figures into the arrangement. The latter number carries historical weight, as it was named for the Manhattan neighbourhood erased by urban renewal. This memory music, proud, bittersweet and defiant, is captured vocally, both separately and together, by Martinez, Almonte and Bosch, with the upper-register trumpet work delivered by Nathaniel Williford. "Raise Four" ignites the band's adventurous side, full of rhythmic displacement and ensemble interplay. Trumpeter Jesus Ricardo cuts through with fire and precision over Martinez's slap, open tone, and muted stroke. Pianist Rodriguez and alto saxophonist Ted Nash make their presence felt throughout the ensemble. "Green Chimney" arrives with buoyant, almost playful energy, capitalizing on Henriquez's big, bold tone throughout the number. As the band transforms Monk's quirky composition into a number that maintains a relaxed yet insistent groove, soloists Chris Lewis on tenor saxophone, Marshall Gilkes on trombone, and pianist Robert Rodriguez each add their expressive voices to the arrangement. The closing track pairs Henriquez's "Plena Azul" with Monk's "Blue Monk," beautifully tying the project together. Almonte and Bosch infuse the performance with a communal spirit as their voices weave naturally through the plena rhythms and blues-infused ensemble lines. Over this celebratory pulse, Dion Tucker and trumpeter Kali Rodriguez-Peña add intensity and spontaneity, deepening the sense of cultural continuity. This album does not merely reinterpret Monk but reveals that he was closer to the clave than many listeners had thought.

items.body: Norwegian jazz pianist and composer Kjetil Andre Mulelid was born on February 4th 1991, in Hurdal, Norway. In 2014, he completed his studies at the Jazz program at Norwegian University of Science and Technology in Trondheim. Thereafter, he has been active with such bands as Kjemile, Wako and others, as well as his own work with Kjetil Mulelid Trio and his duo with Siril Malmedal Hauge. Hauge, a Norwegian jazz singer, was born on November 28th 1992. She was also educated on the jazz program at University of Science and Technology in Trondheim. In addition to heading projects such as Fieldfare and Wild Things Run Fast, she has collaberated with other bands and musicians. In 2010, she received the Norwegian Cultural Educational Council (dream scholarship). In recent years, Hauge and Mulelid have established themselves as prominent voices in the Norwegian music scene, with extensive touring, Spellmann nominations, and critically acclaimed releases, which have gained international attention. Hauge and Mulelid have made themselves known in the Norwegian music scene in recent years. With active touring, a Norwegian grammy award nomination, and several album releases praised by the worldwide press, they have distinguished themselves as a bold voice representing the Norwegian music in the 21st century. Since their studies in Trondheim, they have worked regularly together. Both together and individually, Hauge and Mulelid have become important artists of their generation. The two musicians have collaborated in various constellations since 2013, performing at festivals and venues across Norway, including through Siril's solo project. On March 17th, 2023, their debut duo album Blues and Bells (Grappa) was released. In autumn 2022, Hauge and Mulelid formally established their duo and since then they have developed their distinctive interplay and musical language through concerts in countries such as Japan, China, South Korea, Portugal, France, Romania and Norway. As the recording of Mulelid and Haugh below illustrates, they are perfectly suited for one another.

items.body: The history of America is haunted by ghosts of the past. These ghosts transform our present-day landscape, our everyday lives, and inform the very core of our existence. On Alive With Ghosts Today (Edition Records, 2026), saxophonist Chris Potter steps away from the normal high-adrenaline jazz that has signified his recent outings and has instead put together a band designed to feel more like a small-town ensemble, a mixture of jazz and folk, to lead through a suite of tunes that examines the legacy of abolitionist John Brown and his raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859 and begs to ask the question: what have we learned, what can we learn, why are we still, wrestling with these same ghosts from the past? The ensemble Potter has assembled is the key to the album's success. Bill Frisell plays with a spacious grace that wonderfully supports all the musicians. Frisell blends in seamlessly, sliding between the other instruments and adding his own unique voice to the music; his guitar serves as the counterpoint to Potter's lead lines. It is hard to believe that although drummer Nate Smith has played with Potter for many years, this is the first time he has worked with Frisell, they are intuitively locked in as if they had been playing together for years. Bassist Burniss Travis brings a loose, funky "groove" to the proceedings, providing a fluid anchor alongside Smith to form a formidable rhythm section. Potter's playing throughout is profound; he is not just playing; he is issuing a warning that the same discontent that fueled the fire that led to Brown's failed raid to free the enslaved people at Harper's Ferry is still smoldering beneath the surface of society today. On "Osawatomie Brown," the addition of Sara Caswell on violin, Rane Moore on clarinet and Zekkereya El-magharbel on trombone transforms the band from a traditional jazz quartet into something much more strongly suited to the historical weight of the song, adding a sense of tension to the music, almost as if they were a Greek chorus, answering Potter's playing, commenting on it. They bring a mournful, melancholic sound to the song, haunting and passing judgment on the unfolding events of the unsuccessful raid, as Brown now must face the consequences of leading the failed rebellion. Brown's final words before his execution serve as a grim warning that is as true today as it was then. "I, John Brown, am now quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood." In fact, Potter's suite does not so much as play out as a tribute to Brown, but serves as a haunting reminder that these ghosts are still very alive and relevant today. Potter's weary tone throughout the album points to his disbelief that 167 years after Brown's failed raid on Harpers Ferry, we are still caught up in an endless cycle of conflict, doomed to repeat the failures of the past until we rectify the present. Alive With Ghosts Today is not an easy listen, not because it is not a good album; in fact, it is a triumph of artistic vision, but because it demands the listener to do more than "listen." It is a thought-provoking statement from one of the great artists of today, passing judgment on society through the lens of examining the past and demanding that we act to finally put those ghosts to rest so that we can positively impact the society of both today and tomorrow.

items.body: If, for just 52 minutes, one needs to step away from the breach, do not hesitate to push play on Liminal. A Brooklyn conceptualist by way of Sweden and Seattle, "Andetag" (Swedish for "breath") opens flautist/composer Elsa Nilsson's Liminal. But, all things considered, it could have been sequenced anywhere in the playlist given Nilsson's nod to late-night dance floors. Elusive, bluesy and a very danceable dance of equals, Band of Pulses—Nilsson, fellow piano arsonist Santiago Leibson, wiry bassist Marty Kenney and empath drummer Rodrigo Recabarren—bend to Nilsson's will, but not entirely, and that too quickly becomes part of the lasting beauty. If one can pull themselves away from their sound system long enough to imagine each of the eight tracks that make Liminal a complete work of adventure and invent, then earmark the wistful two-step "Capacity;" the probing "Mourning For Two." featuring a fierce, throughway solo by bassist Kenney; the full fledged freak out "Not Said, Not Heard;" and the free form island influence of "Transition State" for the highlight reel. Because in a nutshell, Nilsson's imagist view of things could have been subtitled Elsa's Blue Dance and still hit the nail on the head. Steadfast in the unerring oscillation borne to the quartet, Nilsson quickly goes about her slippery, subversive art. "Yesterday's Promise" is all the proof needed to put that theory to bed. The aforementioned "Capacity" boasts twirling electronics and overdrive. Add the enticing "1 year, 10 months, 3 days for Ahmaud Arbery"—a hopper of a number that not only doubles dares all the slide stepping, hip bending, marathon dancers out there, but whose compositional structure reflects the date, with the first part comprising 24 bars and the second 11 bars (24/11)— and "Stepping Away" to the list of mad exhibitions. With the scale tilted heavily in her favor, Nilsson goes for it all this time, and Liminal immediately becomes a high bar in the flautist's growing body of work. A considerable body of work that includes the still smoldering drive of the Leibson accompanied Quila Quina -40°17'38.21"N, -71°45'68.48"S (ears&eyes, 2024), the Band of Pulses powered Pulses (ears&eyes, 2023), the hypnotic reactions of Cycles of Formation (ears&eyes, 2022); and her Esthesis Quartet 2022 debut (alongside pianist Dawn Clement, bassist Emma Dayhuff, and drummer Tina Raymond), Esthesis Quartet (Orenda Records). In the press one-sheet, Nilsson explains that what she had in mind for Liminal was the idea of the in-betweens, those transitional or initial stages of a process. Maybe so, and hopefully mission accomplished. But what Nilsson, known for her deep research and immersion into what concerns her most, really does is take a deep dive into the blues: those stages of transition between the in-betweens.

items.body: A trumpet player who sings or a singer who plays trumpet? Christine Fawson puts those questions to the test (again) on It Could Happen to You, the fifth recording under her leadership, playing trumpet and singing on every one of the album's 11 carefully-mined selections from the Great American Songbook. The obvious answer is that Fawson is both a trumpet player who sings and a singer who plays trumpet, which would be beside the point if she did not do both so marvelously well. Many another instrumentalist has decided to widen his or her repertoire by adding a voice to the mix, more often than not with less than salutary results. The same cannot be said of Fawson, who is so impressive in either guise that she could make a decent living as a singer (which she has) or trumpet player (ditto). And should she ever need a backup plan, she is also an educator who taught for 14 years at the Berklee College of Music. Most of the tunes on It Could Happen to You are well known, as are their authors, who include Cole Porter, Hoagy Carmichael, Irving Berlin, Rodgers, Hart, and the Gershwin brothers. Fawson sings them basically as written, using rhythmic changes and occasional scatting (as well as the trumpet, often muted) for variety. She is aided and abetted by a blue-chip rhythm section: pianist Tim Ray, bassist Dave Zinno and drummer Casey Scheuerell, each of whom is pivotal to the album's overall temper and ambience. Fawson sings the way she plays trumpet: bright as sunlight, always squarely on-key, with an abundance of warmth and personality. Those indispensable traits hold her in good stead throughout, starting with the album's alluring title song, written by Johnny Burke and Jimmy Van Heusen and introduced by Dorothy Lamour in the 1944 film, And the Angels Sing. Fawson gives Porter's "It's All Right with Me" a merry ride, using the proper blend of discretion and come-hither charm, before tackling what may seem an odd choice, Carmichael and Johnny Mercer's easygoing "Lazybones," which works surprisingly well, thanks in part to superb counterpoint by Ray, who then sits in as Fawson's lone accompanist on Berlin's plaintive "What'll I Do." Fawson comes out scatting on Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart's "My Heart Stood Still," then uses the muted trumpet to announce another Burke and Van Heusen classic, "Like Someone in Love," which was introduced by Dinah Shore in 1944 and popularized a year later by Bing Crosby. She sings the seldom-heard verse on Don Raye and Gene DePaul's "You Don't Know What Love Is" before cruising through Ray's surprisingly upbeat arrangement, and wrings the last ounce of earnestness from Carl Fischer and Bill Carey's "You've Changed." A pair of songs by the Gershwin brothers follow, the first a curiously undervalued treasure, "I Was Doing All Right," from the 1938 film The Goldwyn Follies (superb bass solo by Zinno), the second the far better-known "Oh, Lady Be Good" (wherein Fawson, Ray and Scheurell deliver awesome solos). Fawson neatly wraps the package with another of Porter's many masterworks, "Every Time We Say Goodbye." When it comes to singing, playing trumpet, connecting with her teammates and simply having a wonderful time doing all of the above, Fawson is a tough act to follow, and It Could Happen to You is a clear-cut winner from start to finish.

items.body: Feebles, Fables and Ferns captures a rare duo session between guitarist Mick Goodrick and pianist Fred Hersch. Recorded in August 1988 at Hersch's studio in New York, the album provides an intimate display of the superbly matched improvisational skills of two musicians in full flight. During his career, Goodrick perfected the art of avoiding the spotlight, even when collaborating with artists such as John Surman, Charlie Haden and Gary Burton. He was not prolific as a composer or recording artist, preferring to work behind the scenes, often in educational roles. Yet his innovative approach to improvisation proved influential, with many prominent musicians, among them Julian Lage and Pat Metheny, acknowledging his impact. For over three decades, Hersch's work as a pianist, composer and collaborator has resulted in over 60 albums, either as a leader or co-leader, along with multiple Grammy nominations and a host of awards. He is internationally recognized as one of jazz's most distinctive voices. The album opens with the title track. This was composed by Goodrick and was originally recorded on his debut album In Passing (ECM, 1979). The guitar opens the track, Hersch joins, and soon the instruments are intertwined, spinning and folding solo lines around, each leaving spaces for the other to explore as they move through an array of moods. Hersch's composition "Heartsong" is the central track. The piece has previously been featured in trio format on his 1990 album Heartsongs (Sunnyside) and on his 2001 solo album Songs Without Words (Nonesuch Records). In the duo's hands, the piece becomes a harmonic delight, the instruments exchanging the melody to captivating effect. The whole album is an exercise in listening and responding. This reaches its height on the spontaneous improvisations of "Five Excursions." As Hersch notes, "The highlight to me is just the level of ensemble playing. There was a lot of profound listening going on between the both of us." Alongside the originals are four covers. "Falling Grace" and "Amazing" are both Steve Swallow compositions, with the latter leading in with Goodrick's "Away 10." Its beautiful unfolding melody and improvised passages form another highlight. Johnny Green and Edward Heyman's "Out Of Nowhere" sees melodic fragments eventually merge and Goodrick's solo shimmers through Mal Waldron's "Soul Eyes." These two musicians are so well matched that they conjure something close to magic in this intimate studio session. They interweave their lines, expanding and contracting to build delicate miniatures, tender melodic exchanges and romantic drifts. But there is energy here too, making this pure musical communication of the highest order.
